title: Atlas Identity
summary: A modular identity for a cultural map project — one mark, sixty-four territories, and a numbering system that lets local editors publish without a designer in the room.
alt: Abstract plate: ultramarine contour rings interrupted by a stepped block of squares, a salmon marker dot, and ink baseline rules on ivory.

sections.copy: The Foundation keeps an archive of regional craft techniques — sixty-four territories, each with its own vocabulary. They needed an identity that could absorb new entries without art direction every time. Our answer was a numbering system first and a logo second: every territory gets an index code, a contour signature, and a fixed spot for its local note.

sections.alt: Atlas plate cropped tall: contour rings stacked vertically beside a stepped column of ultramarine squares.
sections.caption: Territory plates — the contour signature is generated from the region's coastline data, then cropped by the numbering system.

sections.copy: The index became the brand. Nobody draws anything new; they simply file it.

The digital side inherits the paper system. Each archive entry renders as a cropped plate — the same artwork, cut by its index position — so the archive reads like one continuous publication instead of sixty-four microsites.

title: Signal Journal
summary: A weekly journal for a slow-news cooperative — a reading surface that treats every article as a printed issue, complete with folios, margin notes and a cover plate.
alt: Abstract plate: a halftone dot matrix dissolving across ivory, one row enlarged into ultramarine squares, an ink waveform and salmon tick marks.

sections.copy: Signal publishes four stories a week and refuses none of them an illustration budget. Instead of photography, every issue gets a generated plate: a dot matrix whose density is driven by the issue number. Readers learn to read the covers the way train spotters read numbers.

sections.alt: Signal plate cropped card: the halftone matrix at full density with a single enlarged row of squares crossing the frame.
sections.caption: Issue covers — density encodes the week; the enlarged row encodes the lead story's position.

sections.copy: A cover should tell you how much time you are about to spend. Ours does it in dots.

The reading layer stays deliberately plain: one measure, one serif, folios in the margin. The motion budget went into a single move — the cover plate cropping itself into the article header as you enter. Everything else is paper turning.

items: Journal system, cover generator, article template

title: Margins Press
summary: A monograph series for a worker-owned press — ledger-line covers set entirely from the type cases they already owned, plus one square of ultramarine.
alt: Abstract plate: stacked ink ledger bars like lines of text, a torn paper edge, and a stepped stair of ultramarine squares crossing the frame.

sections.copy: The Collective prints on a 1972 Heidelberg and owns exactly four typefaces. Rather than fight it, we built the series from their cases: every cover is a ledger of the book's own contents — chapters as bars, appendices as fine rules — torn once, by hand, along the fore-edge.

sections.alt: Margins plate cropped wide: the ledger bars running the full width with the torn edge and the stepped square stair meeting at the right margin.
sections.caption: Cover system — each monograph sets its own table of contents as a bar ledger.

sections.copy: We showed them a sketch in the type they already had. The vote took four minutes.

The ultramarine stair is the only purchased colour — one pass on the press, shared by every title in the series so the shelf reads as a single object. Digital catalogues photograph the spines; nothing was redrawn for screens.

items: Series design, cover system, spine index
